# Hard-to-vary report: “The Natural History of ‘Oumuamua”

## 1. The question, frozen

The paper answers several questions. The one its title and opening make central: **why does 1I/2017 U1 have the properties we saw, and do they force a non-natural origin?**

Range: the object itself, discovery (19 Oct 2017) to the last Hubble point (2 Jan 2018).

Asked: what produced it (forward), and what its properties let us tell (backward). A near-neighbour question — “is there evidence for an alien origin?” — runs through Section 2. I treat it as part of the same question, not a substitute.

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **A** — ‘Oumuamua is a planetesimal (or fragment) ejected from a young planetary system.
- **B** — its outer volatiles were already gone (an *extinct* comet), so it outgasses without a visible tail.
- **C** — the non-gravitational acceleration, A₁r⁻², comes from that outgassing at ~1 kg/s, from ices just below the surface, in large grains.
- **D** — its red colour is ordinary for organic-rich, iron-rich, or space-weathered surfaces.
- **E** — its ≥6:1 elongation came from one of several routes (tidal disruption, fluidisation to a Jacobi ellipsoid, abrasion, a low-speed collision).
- **F** — its tumbling came from disruption, an encounter, or outgassing during the pass.
- **G** — the number density (0.1 au⁻³) is not demonstrably too high.
- **Rival** — an artificial solar sail, deliberately aimed.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| A | **Held** | By the trajectory job: Figure 4 puts the orbit at the predicted values for *detectable inactive* interstellar objects, and that prediction was published eight months before discovery — so it was not tuned on the case. |
| B | **Held if** | Held only by “nothing bright was seen.” The paper admits no observation could have ruled out water outgassing at the needed level. Doubtful job; a water-sensitive search would settle it. |
| C | **Held** | The 1/r² acceleration is the strongest anomaly. Scaling measured 67P mass loss to a 100 m body gives a similar rate. Solar radiation pressure needs a density 3–4 orders of magnitude too low. |
| D | **Loose** | Swap organic-rich for iron-rich for space-weathered: all fit equally. The paper says colour alone is not diagnostic. |
| E | **Unknown** | The paper’s own words: “none can naturally match such an extreme axis ratio (of at least 6:1) within a self-consistent framework.” Settled by any formed body, or any simulation, that reaches 6:1. |
| F | **Held** as a fact (tumbling is seen) / **Unknown** as to origin — two routes offered, neither settled. |
| G | **Held** | Figure 3’s experiment shows the inferred number density moves by orders of magnitude with the assumed size-frequency distribution. The “higher than expected” claim needs an SFD that does not exist yet. |
| Rival (sail) | **Held if** | The separating test is real: a >10:1 sail must stay nearly edge-on while the light curve needs a changing orientation. But the paper’s closing line — “it has not been shown that an orientation exists” — is an absence, and absences stay missing. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip.** Had a bright tail appeared, the same “ejected planetesimal” story would have run, only easier. The headline word “natural” covers both outcomes, so it holds nothing by itself. Part C does not have this fault: the acceleration pins it.
- **Direction.** B and E run backwards from the light curve and the acceleration. C runs forward: 67P scaled down, and the rate the orbit demands. Mixed — say which is which.
- **Answer hidden in the starting points.** “Natural” is close to a label. It earns its keep only where it meets the rival, and there it does — at the light curve.
- **Jobs I added.** “Why is such elongation rare among larger bodies?” is mine, not the paper’s. It answers with a selection effect, which is **held if** that effect is real.
- **Pairs that pull.** E and F fight. One paper says the outgassing needed for C would spin a 6:1 body past break-up; another says outgassing from the sunlit point avoids it. The review reports both and picks neither.
- **Catch-all.** “may have lost most/all of its CO and CO₂ … Alternatively, it may have had intrinsically low abundances” absorbs any volatile non-detection. The gauge would be a pre-perihelion measurement. There is none. No gauge, no catch-all.
- **What the change list leaves out.** No pre-perihelion data; no sensitivity to millimetre grains; no water-sensitive search; the size distribution unknown. The paper states each openly — to its credit.
- **Borrowed parts.** Much is borrowed: the 67P scaling, the ejection simulations, every SFD. Each rests on a separate explanation not tested here.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

Two. **One:** a pre-perihelion observation of the next interstellar object, with a water-sensitive search. That fixes B and closes the volatile catch-all. **Two:** any self-consistent route to a ≥6:1 body of known formation. That fixes E — the paper’s own open question.

## 6. What this does not show

Passing is not truth. A well-held explanation can still be wrong; ‘Oumuamua could be a sail, and this test would not say so. It also cannot judge whether the review is complete — only which parts are pinned and which are not.

## 7. One next step

Write down, before LSST’s first detection, what a natural object and an artificial one would each show. Figure 4 is that, done once, eight months early — and it worked.
